papers.abstract: We characterize bipartite graphs whose edge rings are almost Gorenstein. Using this characterization, we recover known results for two families of graphs. In addition, we show that if the edge ring of a bipartite graph is almost Gorenstein and its $h$-polynomial has degree at least two, then the $h$-polynomial is palindromic except possibly for the linear and next-to-leading coefficients. Moreover, we construct two bipartite graphs whose edge rings have the same $h$-vector, although only one of the rings is almost Gorenstein.

papers.title: Forecasting Visitor Demand from Open AI-Camera Counts and Weather: Lessons from Japan for Saudi Heritage Sites
papers.abstract: Small heritage and nature sites need a few days' notice of busy days to plan staff, overflow parking and shuttles, but most have neither sensors nor forecasting expertise. We test what one artificial intelligence (AI) camera counter per site, a public holiday calendar and a free weather forecast can predict. Using 22 months of open AI-camera counts from three contrasting sites in Fukui, Japan (a train station, a coastal cliff and a mountain summit park), we measure how weather changes visits, forecast daily counts up to a week ahead with only the weather forecast available at the time, test busy-day warnings tied to a staffing decision, and ask how much history a new counter needs. The more exposed the site, the more weather matters: 10 mm of rain comes with 3% fewer detections at the station, 9% fewer at the cliff and 37% fewer at the summit park. With the forecasts actually issued, three-day-ahead weighted absolute percentage error (WAPE) at the summit park falls from 38.5% to 31.9% (Diebold-Mariano p<0.001), and the gain holds to five days; the sheltered station gains nothing. Three-day busy-day warnings with forecast weather reach, on past data and under the primary definitions, an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.87-0.93, and weather lifts the overflow car park warning's precision from 0.60 to 0.82. For a new counter, blending a learned model with last week's same-hour counts cuts hourly error after only three days of training, pending a real installation. All inputs are off the shelf, and we outline how the approach could apply to heritage sites in Saudi Arabia.

papers.title: Alternative Tikhonov-Type Regularization for the Calderón Inverse Conductivity Problem
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the application of two regularization methods, classical Tikhonov and Alternative Tikhonov regularization, to the Calderón inverse conductivity problem. We develop an iterative reconstruction scheme based on linearizing the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map and approximating conductivity updates using Gaussian basis functions. The resulting linear systems are solved using both regularization methods, with particular attention given to the derivation and numerical implementation of Alternative Tikhonov regularization. We compare the performance of these methods through numerical experiments on a synthetic conductivity containing two localized regions of differing conductivity. A total of 666 reconstruction tests are performed across varying regularization parameters, damping factors, and iteration counts. The lowest relative reconstruction errors obtained are 0.064730 for Alternative Tikhonov and 0.065173 for classical Tikhonov regularization. Although both methods produce comparable reconstructions, Alternative Tikhonov achieves the lowest observed error. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of both approaches within the proposed reconstruction scheme and motivate further investigation into parameter selection, numerical stability, and reconstruction accuracy.

papers.title: Self-Normalized Inference from Riemannian Stochastic Gradient Paths
papers.abstract: Riemannian stochastic gradient paths estimate constrained parameters, but confidence regions usually require estimating the Hessian and gradient-noise covariance. We develop self-normalized inference from one path by expressing retained iterates in a common random tangent space. Their average and centered partial sums share an unknown covariance factor that cancels in a Brownian bridge pivot. Under suitable regularity conditions, a joint expansion of the averaged estimator and integrated path controls nonlinear coordinate errors using conditional second moments. The procedure uses fixed-dimensional memory and extends to nondegenerate smooth functionals and alternative local coordinates. Numerical studies show competitive coverage relative to plug-in Wald inference while avoiding Hessian and residual-density estimation.

papers.title: Nonlinear kink modes for nonisentropic supersonic vortex sheets
papers.abstract: In this paper, planar nonisentropic vortex sheets of the two-dimensional Euler equations under the stability condition are studied via nonlinear geometric optics, focusing on the interaction induced by a small-amplitude, high-frequency incident wave impinging on a planar vortex sheet. It is found that there exist three asymmetric critical incident angles at which resonance occurs, leading to a significant amplification of the reflected and refracted oscillatory waves. Moreover, by refining the asymptotic expansion, we deduce that the leading profiles of the highly oscillatory waves are described by initial-boundary value problems for Burgers transport equations, while the leading profile of the contact discontinuity front satisfies an initial value problem for a Hamilton--Jacobi-type equation, which reduces to a forced linear transport equation on one resonant branch. These results extend the resonant amplification mechanism from the isentropic setting to the nonisentropic Euler flow and reveal the asymmetric influence of entropy variations on the nonlinear evolution of compressible vortex sheets.

papers.title: Contracting for Experimentation with Private Findings
papers.abstract: A principal hires an agent to work on a project of unknown quality. Success is contractible, but before it occurs, the agent may privately obtain a favorable finding. For example, a scientist developing a drug may observe a promising microscope reading. An informed agent may conceal the finding; an uninformed agent may fake one. The agent's private information could guide both the project's duration and his pay. Yet I show that an optimal contract pays only success bonuses tied to time, not reported findings, consistent with time-based payment schedules often used in research funding. Dynamically arriving private information drives this simplicity: the agent can conceal good news to retain higher bonuses, so deterring concealment limits pay differences across report histories. Bonuses are high and rising in a research stage that induces learning, then fall to a low, constant level in a development stage where only an informed agent continues working. Rising bonuses reflect a novel force: rents from private learning motivate effort but shrink as fewer research periods remain.

papers.title: HALO-LP: A Homogeneous All-Shifted Non-Interior-Point Method for Linear Programming
papers.abstract: This letter introduces HALO-LP, a novel homogeneous all-shifted non-interior-point method for linear programming (LP). The proposed method combines a homogeneous self-dual (HSD) embedding with all-shifted nonlinear complementarity (NCP) functions and proximal primal-dual regularization, enabling arbitrary primal-dual warm starts without requiring strictly interior iterates. The resulting Newton equations admit a condensation based on a positive-definite matrix that can be efficiently factorized using Cholesky decomposition, while the HSD embedding enables primal and dual infeasibility detection through Farkas certificates. Numerical evaluations on perturbed LP instances derived from the Netlib test set demonstrate state-of-the-art warm-starting performance, outperforming the competing solvers in the evaluated setting. We further validate optimality and infeasibility detection on analytically characterized LP problems. Finally, we demonstrate HALO-LP's applicability to robotic optimal control through sequential linear programming (SLP) for centroidal walking and trotting of quadrupedal robots.

papers.title: pico-WAM: Evaluating Counterfactual Prediction and Planning Error in a Compact World Action Model
papers.abstract: When a World Action Model fails at control, is the bottleneck proposal generation or trajectory scoring? We introduce pico-WAM, a compact model with supplied physical state for tracing policy-dynamics interactions. Using 206 Push-T demonstrations and 15 training seeds, we compare data regimes and search configurations. Counterfactual branch training improves short-horizon cost ranking and enlarges the coverage advantage of policy-restarted over warm-started search by 4.8 percentage points; restart wins under both data regimes. Replacing learned trajectory scores with simulator costs improves coverage by 12.2 points while retaining learned proposals. Substituting simulator states in proposal generation alone shows no detected gain. Component diagnostics and a separate door-opening study show why better ranking need not yield better control or outperform imitation. These controlled interventions identify scoring as an effective improvement target in the tested setting and provide a reproducible protocol for diagnosing compact world models.

papers.title: ParaBlock++: Communication-Computation Parallel Blockwise Hierarchical Federated Learning
papers.abstract: In the emerging 6G paradigm, where AI-driven services operate over decentralized and resource-constrained infrastructures, the convergence of distributed learning algorithms remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces $\mathrm{ParaBlock}$++, a low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite-assisted hierarchical federated learning (HFL) framework, enabling resource-limited terrestrial clients to collaboratively engage in federated learning (FL) via ground-satellite links (GSLs) supported by LEO satellite megaconstellations. Within this architecture, LEO satellites serve multiple roles: as edge servers aggregating and broadcasting models, as clients accelerating training, and as high-throughput relays managing inter-satellite routing through inter-satellite links (ISLs). Departing from conventional synchronous Jacobian-type updates, $\mathrm{ParaBlock}$++ employs asynchronous BCD-type updates to enhance convergence speed. We provide theoretical convergence guarantees for convex, strongly convex, and non-convex objectives, and formulate optimization problems to determine optimal cluster resource allocation and model partitioning for minimizing global training latency. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that $\mathrm{ParaBlock}$++ achieves faster initial convergence and comparable final performance for deep neural networks (DNNs) such as ResNet-18, offering promising directions for federated learning across geographically remote areas enabled by 6G technologies, but much less global rounds and communication cost.

papers.title: Impact Mechanism of a Point Interaction in the Cubic Half-Wave Equation: Well-Posedness, Constrained Energy Levels and Near-Critical Rigidity
papers.abstract: We study the one-dimensional nonlinear half-wave equation with a logarithmically renormalized point interaction. The nonlinearity is focusing and cubic, which is mass-critical. We establish well-posedness in the energy space using a new method for unconditional uniqueness that requires no auxiliary Strichartz assumption. We reveal the mechanism by which the point interaction affects ground states. The free critical mass is the sharp threshold: fixed-mass ground states exist and are orbitally stable below it, whereas at and above it the constrained energy is unbounded from below. We also prove a near-critical rigidity result showing that bounded energy concentrating sequences converge to free ground states after rescaling.

papers.title: Constraint Dependency Graph Retrieval for Compliance Detection on Long SKILL Documents
papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents carry out business operations under enterprise documents we refer to as SKILL documents, which take the form of standard operating procedures (SOPs) that state the conditions to verify and the actions to take before an operation proceeds. Long, densely cross-referenced SKILL documents exceed the context budget of small deployed auditors. Similarity-based retrieval then brings in irrelevant rules while omitting mandatory prerequisites, and the two-stage audit policy provides no trainable signal for the retrieval stage. We present SkillCDG, a compliance detection framework that reformulates each SKILL document as a constraint dependency graph, shifting rule retrieval from similarity-based matching to closure-based selection under the deployment's context budget. Each atomic rule is anchored to its source text span as a graph node, and mandatory prerequisite relations form the sole edge type. Policy-generated retrieval keywords activate seed rules, whose dependency closure yields a compact and conditionally complete rule context within that budget. The same graph also supports a joint optimization scheme. The retrieval stage is trained with group-relative policy optimization using a verifiable reward that combines output-format validity with downstream verdict correctness, with closure non-emptiness serving as a validity gate, while selective on-policy distillation concentrates teacher supervision on high-entropy reasoning tokens, with verdict and termination tokens always included, to improve verdict accuracy. Experiments on three enterprise datasets and two public benchmarks show that SkillCDG improves accuracy and F1 over the full-document and retrieval-based baselines.

papers.title: Dependable Agents Need Hard and Fuzzy Rules
papers.abstract: Language models let software read requests in ordinary language, but they keep rules as people do: usually, and less so under pressure. Conventional code keeps rules exactly, but it cannot read a request. We argue that dependable agents need both, because the two kinds of rule cover overlapping and unequal regions of what an agent might do. Code holds the limits that can be stated exactly. Learned fuzzy rules cover the judgment that cannot. We test the hard layer in three domains, purchasing, delegation of authority and data access, on 1,340 episodes written by authors outside our team. Models left to decide for themselves executed unauthorized actions in up to 151 of 340 purchasing episodes and 269 of 470 delegation episodes, and the strongest model breached in every condition. A hard guard between proposal and action executed none, and an exhaustive search of 183,204 proposals agreed. In a further test, where an outsider wrote the owner's rules and a program mapped them to the guard, two episodes breached at a boundary we had written down in advance. We then test the pair. Concept Programming instills a named rule in a model and measures its errors on wording it never saw. A small model taught four judgment rules this way flagged 95 of 96 rule-breaking purchases that no exact rule can see, and 4 of 108 legitimate requests. Placed in front of the guard, it left 1 of 192 rule-breaking requests unstopped, where the guard alone left 77 and 70, and the guard still held every exact limit. A prompted frontier model did about as well, so the claim is that a small taught rule can do the job, not that it does it better.

papers.title: Building Weighted PubMed Citation Graphs at Scale: A Pipeline and an Audit of Edge-Similarity Features
papers.abstract: Studies of scientific literature often combine citation links with article metadata, but the data preparation needed to do so at the scale of millions of papers is laborious and error-prone. This paper describes a pipeline that turns PubMed metadata and a citation network into a graph whose edges carry seven similarity features: bibliographic coupling and co-citation (each as a count and as a Jaccard coefficient), publication-year proximity, MeSH-term similarity, and similarity of MedCPT title-abstract embeddings. Applied to a citation network derived from the cell biology research literature, the pipeline yields 7,445,898 nodes and 57,512,086 edges with complete year, MeSH, title, and abstract metadata. The paper reports how nodes are matched across sources, how duplicate identifiers are resolved, and which intermediate tables grew to hundreds of gigabytes. An audit of the full feature table shows that 47.2% of the edges share neither references nor citing documents, so their topological features are zero, and that the MeSH feature is nonzero on only 0.28% of edges. Where both kinds of signal exist, they agree: edges with higher coupling also have more similar abstracts and closer publication years. In a pilot, replacing the median by a mean or best-match aggregation makes the MeSH feature nonzero on nearly all article pairs, and near-identical texts point to possible duplicate records that identifier checks miss. The parsing, graph-construction, and feature code are public; the paper states which data are released and which are not. A companion paper uses the resulting weighted graph for clustering.

papers.title: Investigating ET-SoC-1 Vector and Parallel Performance with sGEMM
papers.abstract: The Ainekko (formerly Esperanto) ET-SoC-1 is a massively parallel RISC-V accelerator. Its compute array comprises 1024 dual-threaded in-order ET-Minion cores (2048 harts) operating at 600 MHz, each core providing an eight-lane 256-bit packed-single (PS) SIMD datapath shared by its two harts, with access to LPDDR4X memory at a nominal 133 GiB/s. This paper presents a performance investigation using single-precision general matrix multiplication (sGEMM) as the benchmark kernel. Two device kernels are implemented and evaluated on the ET-SoC-1, these are a register-blocked PS SIMD baseline with two-step software pipelining, and a TensorFMA32 kernel that drives the same FMA datapath through the per-core tensor micro-operation sequencer, with double-buffered A scratchpad loading. Because both kernels are bounded by the same arithmetic peak, the comparison isolates the effect of operand delivery from that of arithmetic width. Performance is compared against CPU references (SpacemiT K3, Intel i5-11600, AMD Ryzen 9 9950X and the Arm Cortex-X925/A725 CPU of an NVIDIA DGX Spark) and two GPUs (NVIDIA GB10 Blackwell and AMD RDNA4 RX 9060 XT).

papers.title: Entropy-Regularized Reinforcement Learning for the Regime-Switching Consumption-Investment Problem
papers.abstract: This paper establishes an entropy-regularized reinforcement learning (ERRL) framework for the continuous-time consumption-investment problem under a regime-switching market model with general utility functions. By incorporating randomized exploratory policies and Shannon entropy regularization into the stochastic optimal control formulation, we derive closed-form representations for the optimal exploratory consumption and investment strategies. Specifically, the optimal investment strategy follows a multivariate Gaussian distribution, whereas the optimal consumption strategy takes the form of a Gibbs measure---which specializes to a Gamma distribution under logarithmic utility and a non-standard exponential distribution under power utility. Crucially, our theoretical analysis reveals that the classical deterministic optimal decisions correspond to the mode---rather than the mean---of these exploratory distributions. Furthermore, we establish the convergence of the exploratory value function to its classical unregularized counterpart as the temperature parameter vanishes. For algorithmic design, we develop a continuous-time q-learning framework grounded in a novel continuous-time q-function, prove the policy improvement theorem, and establish martingale characterizations for both on-policy and off-policy learning. We find that parameterizing the actor network based on theoretical distribution families can help accelerate convergence and enhance numerical stability. Furthermore, numerical experiments across regime-switching environments provide empirical support for our theoretical findings, demonstrating stable loss convergence as well as the monotonicity and concavity of the learned value functions.

papers.title: How Close to the Theme? Similarity-Label Conditioning for Game Music Generation
papers.abstract: Composers develop music from an original idea, controlling how similar each new section is to it, from near repetition to new material. Game music needs this often, as its material repeats over long play. Music models, however, rarely learn to control similarity from real pieces. We further train a pretrained MIDI model on section pairs from Super Mario pieces. A label states each pair's similarity, and a context vector summarises the given section, or context. For 157 test contexts, the model generates six outputs per label. Twelve measures score the outputs; one main measure each covers melody, pitch content, rhythm and note length. On average, outputs requested as similar are more similar to their context than those requested as dissimilar, and not to other pieces. All twelve measures favour them; each main measure stays significant after correction for multiple tests. On melody, the gap comes mainly from more frequent restatement of the context's melody. Against an otherwise identical model without a label, only the request for high similarity makes outputs more similar. In a listening test, ratings followed melodic overlap with the context most closely of all measures.

papers.title: Infinite Worlds from One Example: What Local Generators Must Share
papers.abstract: Seeded noise lets games generate any region of an unbounded world on demand. We ask what such a generator needs when every small window must come from one example, the constraint behind Wave Function Collapse. The difficulty is that local constraints can require agreement over arbitrary distances: in a brick wall, each row keeps its place between the mortar lines. We study local generators, each cell a fixed function of the randomness near it. When the constraints carry a quantity that varies across the example, no generator that applies one rule, ignoring position, to independent randomness at every cell can be both exactly valid and faithful to the example's statistics, however far each cell reads. At radius r, staying faithful forces forbidden windows at a density of at least order 1/r, and a construction attains this order. To vary the quantity between exactly valid worlds, a generator needs randomness shared along its direction. We give a finitely checkable condition under which row types drawn from the seed and the position modulo a fixed period suffice for exact validity without learning. A search over the example's patches certifies these quantities and names the input each needs. Across 52 public examples of Wave Function Collapse and 27 from other implementations, it certifies only examples where a learned generator on independent randomness stays far from valid after repair. Given that input, a neural cellular automaton and a diffusion model become valid on 10 and 8 of the 12 certified examples that receive one, and on none from independent randomness. Valid means at most one forbidden window in a thousand after repair. With octaves of seeded noise elsewhere, the automaton is valid on 45 of the 52 public examples and 21 of the 27 from other implementations, and repair keeps random access.

papers.title: Similarity-Weighted Leiden-CPM Clustering of a 7.4-Million-Node Biomedical Citation Graph: Weight Alignment, Scale, and Sparsity
papers.abstract: Clustering citation networks into research communities supports science mapping, research evaluation, and the analysis of funding portfolios. Biomedical articles also carry metadata, such as MeSH terms, publication year, and abstracts, that can be turned into similarity-based edge weights for Leiden clustering under the Constant Potts Model (CPM). Studies of hybrid relatedness compare the accuracy of such clusterings, but how the weights interact with the CPM resolution parameter on a large graph is less clear. Here it is shown that, on a citation network derived from the cell biology research literature (7.4 million nodes, 57.5 million edges), the effect of the weights is governed mainly by their scale and by edges of weight zero, and that, once these are controlled, weighting gives modestly more coherent clusters. Edges were weighted with seven topological and semantic similarity features and clustered with Leiden-CPM, using a method updated to fix a bug in how earlier code attached weights to edges. Mean weights of 0.0015 to 0.23 raised the effective resolution 4- to 650-fold; dividing by the mean restored most of the coverage, except for topological weightings, in which the 47% of edges with weight zero hold most of it. At equal coverage, weighted clusters were more coherent than unweighted ones, also on features outside the weight. For weighted CPM clustering, weights should therefore be attached to edges by key, normalized or reported with their effective resolution, and checked for zero-weight edges.

papers.title: Adaptive Land Units from Earth Embeddings
papers.abstract: Modeling land use starts with a choice of spatial units, typically a regular grid of pixels whose resolution is set by the spatial detail the process requires and, often more critically, by the computational budget. With Earth observation data more abundant than ever, we ask whether good land units can instead emerge from the data itself. To do that, we cluster AlphaEarth embeddings with a parallel Bayesian hierarchical clustering into adaptive land units, large where the land is uniform and small where it is highly heterogeneous. Using Denmark as a case study, we turn 402M land pixels into 1.27M newly defined units, about 320 times fewer, without any labels (i.e., unsupervised), making it possible to fit the whole country on a single consumer-grade GPU. Importantly, these units describe the land well, as a regular grid needs about 5 times as many cells to match them against land-use labels, and about 4 times as many against the declared crop of every field. Compared to clustering the satellite images themselves, the embeddings need half the units for the same purity. But more notably, they work as modeling units. Land-use maps learned on them are within a few points of accuracy of pixel models at a small fraction of the cost, and they make whole-country land-use estimates with reliable uncertainty possible in under a minute, where the same model on pixels does not even fit in device memory.

papers.title: Two types of averaging principles for multiplicative stochastic Korteweg-de Vries equations with fast oscillations
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study averaging principles for stochastic KdV equations perturbed by a fast oscillating term generated by a stochastic reaction-diffusion equation in $H^s(\mathbb{R})$, $ s\geq 0$. When dealing with multilinear estimates of the nonlinear terms in the stochastic KdV type equation, two kinds of workspace are both effective. The classical workspace can help us prove the averaging principle in the $L_ω^2$ sense, but it has more restrictions on the noise kernel and the conservation structures. When we use a new workspace without homogeneous low frequency restrictions, only the regularity conditions and the $L_x^2$ conservation structure is needed. Correspondingly, because there is no moment estimate of the solution, we can only prove the perturbed equations converge to an averaging equation in the probability sense. Our works may have important reference value, because it not only provides a new perspective to handle dynamical problems of stochastic dispersive model, but also compare it with the classical method.

papers.title: Unlocking Low-Frequency Laser Doppler Holography Spectra for Functional Retinal and Choroidal Microvascular Phenotyping
papers.abstract: The low-frequency part of optical fluctuation spectra recorded by laser Doppler holography at a frame rate of 37~kHz is typically filtered out to reveal functional blood-flow waveforms in major retinal and choroidal vessels. We construct a time-varying spectral-excess (SE) distribution in capillary-associated territories by selecting complete cardiac cycles and applying successive spatial and beat medians in regions where vessels are unresolved and intermittent eye motion can dominate the signal. At each phase, spectral excess compares the integrated Doppler spectral area between two fixed low-frequency peaks near $\pm2$~kHz with a reference area defined by the high-frequency tail near $\pm18.5$~kHz. The resulting waveform, displayed against normalized cardiac phase, retains variation throughout the cardiac cycle and provides a basis for exploring its temporal organization. We summarize spectral-excess strength by the spectral excess index (SEI), defined as the temporal median of SE, and also describe an alternative evaluation after spectral pooling. A representative recording illustrates the construction. Physiological specificity and repeatability remain to be quantified.

papers.title: Efficient Conformal Calibration for Paired Recommendation Decisions
papers.abstract: Risk control can suppress useful changes to a frozen recommendation rule. We study how to recover valid activation from the same observed fractional losses. Two specified internal calibrators can lose efficiency by compressing losses into their sum or clipping auxiliary inverse counts before averaging. We propose Averaged Conformal Risk Calibration, or ACRC, which averages before clipping. A product identity proves expected-risk validity, while pointwise bounds characterize the additional activation. For fixed populations sampled without replacement, we connect activation to signed utility under heterogeneous users and switching constraints. Near the budgets, positive population mean gain and the stated nondegeneracy conditions give positive leading-order utility increments despite sampling dependence. Across six datasets, changing only calibration improves discounted net utility by $0.010226$ over raw and $0.008337$ over RB. A separately frozen Jester confirmation gives $0.011025 \pm 0.001082$ over raw with the rule and filter fixed, using a five-seed approximate 95 percent paired interval. Against information-matched SCoRE selecting risk or reward scores, the mean utility difference is $+0.015934 \pm 0.001440$. These gains use more mean realized risk within the declared budgets. Upstream failures delimit the benefit: efficient calibration releases useful modifications when the proposals themselves have value.

papers.title: Finite-Time Tracking Success or Failure in the Pursuer--Evader Model
papers.abstract: We investigate a sufficient framework for determining the success or failure of finite-time tracking in pursuer--evader dynamics. To this end, we design a nonsmooth coupled multi-agent system by adopting a previously established pursuer--evader model from the existing literature, which characterizes asymptotic tracking success and failure, as the backbone. We then provide appropriate sufficient conditions, expressed in terms of initial data, system parameters, and kernel functionals, under which some pursuers can successfully track evaders within a finite time, while others fail to do so. In particular, we show that the pursuer--evader subsystem associated with the pursuers that successfully track the evader, together with the corresponding evaders, exhibits finite-time stability.

papers.title: Nonnegative Rank Bounds for the Algebraic Monotone Calculus
papers.abstract: In Hrubes' Algebraic Monotone Calculus a DNF tautology $A$ is proved by a monotone arithmetic circuit computing $χ(A)-εχ(1)$ for some $ε>0$, where the coefficient of $χ(A)$ at $x^σ$ counts the terms of $A$ satisfied by $σ$, and $χ(1)=\prod_i(x_i^0+x_i^1)$. Proof size is circuit size, and $ε$ is existentially quantified, so lower bounds must hold at arbitrarily small $ε$. We prove lower bounds for bounded-depth fragments by two nonnegative rank measures of the target: monotone tensor rank and the nonnegative rank of a flattening. At depth three a proof is a nonnegative tensor decomposition. Restricting its terms to subcube indicators gives conical juntas, a system polynomially equivalent to Sherali-Adams in twin variables. For arbitrary terms we adapt Rothvoss' hyperplane separation to monotone tensor rank: Tseitin formulas on constant-degree expanders of large girth need proofs of size $2^{Ω(εn)}$ whenever $ε=ω(\log n/n)$. This cannot reach every $ε$: at shift $2^{-Θ(n\log n)}$ Tseitin acquires polynomial-size depth-three proofs, separating the two fragments exponentially. A constant-size index gadget gives bounds for every $ε\geq2^{-Ω(n)}$, converting a Sherali-Adams degree bound into a size bound. Depth three is essential: Tseitin has monotone proofs of size $O(n^3)$ and depth $O(\log n)$ at every $ε$. Beyond depth three we bound the nonnegative rank of a flattening by $L^{2^t}$ for a monotone formula with $L$ leaves and mixed-product depth $t$: the largest number of product gates on a root-to-leaf path whose two inputs each meet both sides of the bipartition. Approximate extension complexity then bounds perfect matching and odd factor instances, and planted CSP integrality gaps give an explicit family of planted Tseitin DNFs hard at inverse-polynomial shift.

papers.title: Universal Threshold Memory in Bound-State Recapture
papers.abstract: Driven slowly, a quantum system forgets how it was driven. We show that a bound state taken slowly to its continuum threshold and back does not. The recaptured fraction depends on the ratio of the approach and return rates, however slow both are. The two rates set the sizes of two threshold packets whose phase-sensitive overlap fixes recapture. Common slowing preserves their size ratio. A factorized treatment of approach and return misses this dependence. For a short-range $s$-wave state whose inverse scattering length touches zero quadratically in time, we obtain the dependence in closed form, with the maximum $1/\varphi^2$ at matched rates, where $\varphi$ is the golden ratio. A ratio of three recaptured fractions makes this threshold memory accessible with finite pulses. For radio-frequency-dressed $^{85}$Rb halo dimers with half-pulse widths of 30 and $120~μ$s, coupled-channel calculations give this ratio within $0.5\%$ of its slow-limit value.

papers.title: Quantitative Analytical Spheroid Model for Scattering-Type Scanning Near-Field Optical Spectroscopy of Layered Samples
papers.abstract: Scattering-type scanning near-field optical microscopy (s-SNOM) is a versatile tool for probing optical properties at deeply subwavelength scales. Its theoretical modeling, however, typically relies on computationally intensive numerical simulations or phenomenological analytical models, limiting quantitative spectral interpretation. In our previous work, we introduced an exact analytical solution for the quasi-electrostatic prolate spheroid model of s-SNOM for homogeneous bulk samples, combining the accuracy of numerical simulations with the efficiency of analytical approaches. Here, we generalize this framework to multilayer samples using two equivalent methods: a generalized image charge method and a Fourier integral method. The resulting exact spheroid model reproduces finite-element simulations within numerical precision while retaining the computational efficiency of an analytical model. We validate the model experimentally for poly (methyl methacrylate) layers of different thicknesses, showing that a single set of geometrical parameters simultaneously reproduces multiple demodulation harmonics and all measured thicknesses, unlike the finite dipole model. We further demonstrate its applicability to strongly resonant SiC layers on dielectric and photoexcited InAs substrates, where existing analytical approaches fail. The model provides an efficient quantitative framework for interpreting multilayer s-SNOM spectra and extracting local optical properties.

papers.title: A characterization and closure property of Thorin's class
papers.abstract: Thorin's class coincides with the smallest class of probability laws on $\mathbb{R}$ that contains all gamma laws and their reflections, while being closed under convolution and weak convergence. In particular, all Thorin laws are self-decomposable. This paper proves an alternative characterization of Thorin's class in terms of what we call the hyperbolic Bochner-Bernstein property. This property corresponds to the notion of hyperbolically completely monotone Laplace transforms on the positive half line, but extended to the real-valued setting. Using the new characterization, it is shown that Thorin's class is closed under multiplication with independent random variables admitting hyperbolically completely monotone densities, which partly settles an open question raised by Bondesson and allows for proving that a large class of possibly skewed real-valued distributions is in Thorin's class. As particular examples, we apply the closure property to show that Johnson's S\textsubscript{U} distribution and the Pearson type IV distribution are in Thorin's class for all parameter choices.

papers.title: Temperature, Not Knowledge: What Recursive Self-Training and Its Remedies Do to a Language Model's Confidence
papers.abstract: Recursive self-training can collapse language models, and many proposed remedies target overconfidence, yet their effects on confidence are rarely measured. We study a five-round self-training loop on Qwen3-1.7B, using three seeds per compared method, and distinguish confidence temperature (drift from a calibrated starting point) from discrimination (ranking correct answers above incorrect ones). Accuracy and overall discrimination remain nearly unchanged, but confidence sharpens and the most confident answers become less reliable. Matching predictive entropy to the calibrated starting model each round recalibrates nearly as well as label-based temperature fitting, at both 1.7B and 8B. Sharpening is not inherent to self-training: exact samples from a model's distribution have zero expected gradient. Instead, most drift comes from fitting each generated answer twice, with top-p truncation contributing the rest; removing both keeps entropy on generated outputs flat. Remedies affect the two properties differently: truncated cross-entropy, an entropy bonus, and single-pass training preserve temperature without improving discrimination, while focal loss and multi-sample targets improve discrimination but cause underconfidence. Reference-data mixing also overshoots. Pairing a ranking-improving loss with label-free recalibration achieves both.

papers.title: A local limit theorem for singularity visits on translation surfaces
papers.abstract: Let $(X,ω)$ be a translation surface with at least one singularity. We investigate the distribution of the number of singularity encounters along prime closed geodesics on $X$. Writing $\ell(γ)$ for the geometric length of a closed geodesic and $m(γ)$ for the number of singularities it encounters, we establish a uniform counting local limit theorem for the values of $m(γ)$ sampled over $\ell(γ)<T$. The key technical step is to introduce and study a trace-class operator whose spectral data encodes the Fourier transform of our counting distribution. Our results hold for every translation surface, without genericity assumptions.

papers.title: Appointed-Time Fault-Tolerant Fast Terminal Sliding Control for UAVs with a Tracking Error-Based Disturbance Observer
papers.abstract: This paper addresses the critical challenge of high-performance fault-tolerant tracking control for quadrotor UAVs under complex conditions including external disturbances, parameter uncertainties, and actuator faults. A synergistic control framework is proposed by decoupling the system into position and attitude loops, each governed by the following three innovations. First, an Appointed-Time Prescribed Performance Function (AT-PPF) is developed to strictly constrain the tracking error within a predefined funnel boundary, ensuring convergence within a fixed time regardless of initial conditions. Second, a Tracking Error-Based Fixed-Time Composite Disturbance Observer (TFxTCDO) is developed to enable fast and accurate estimation of lumped disturbances without requiring full-state information or precise system modeling. This observer directly couples disturbance estimation with the control objective, thereby enhancing robustness and convergence. Third, a Fast Second-Order Terminal Sliding Mode Controller (NFSO-TSMC) is designed to achieve faster convergence and effective chattering mitigation. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed control strategy significantly outperforms conventional methods in terms of tracking accuracy, fault recovery speed, and robustness against uncertainties.

papers.title: A smaller kernel for Ptolemaic Vertex Deletion
papers.abstract: In the Ptolemaic Vertex Deletion problem, the input consists of an undirected graph $G$ and an integer $k$. The goal is to decide whether there is a set of at most $k$ vertices whose removal from $G$ results in a Ptolemaic graph. In this paper, we give a kernel for Ptolemaic Vertex Deletion with $O(k^5)$ vertices. Our result improves upon the $O(k^6)$ kernel of Agrawal et al. [IPEC 2021].

papers.title: Robust Reward Machine Learning and Execution in Noisy Environments
papers.abstract: Background: Reward machines (RMs) represent non-Markovian reward functions as finite-state machines over high-level propositional events. Traditionally, these events are generated by a deterministic labelling function that maps environment states to proposition sets. However, real-world labelling functions are inherently noisy. Objectives: Design and implement a method that learns RMs in the presence of noisy labelling functions and exploits them for policy learning in both discrete and continuous environments. Methods: We propose Prob-IRM, a method that learns RMs from noisy proposition histories using inductive logic programming (ILP) and exploits them for policy learning. Noisy proposition histories are represented as training examples for ILP, which learns an RM that maximises coverage of low-uncertainty histories. RM learning is interleaved with policy optimisation. Prob-IRM uses a belief over RM states to determine when to relearn the RM and to provide additional guiding rewards. Results: Prob-IRM is evaluated on environments with discrete and continuous state spaces under varying levels of labelling noise. Prob-IRM performs comparably to baselines using handcrafted RMs and outperforms approaches that use recurrent neural networks to encode history, despite operating with noisy labels. Conclusions: Prob-IRM represents a step towards deploying reward machines in noisy, real-world environments.

papers.title: Maximal input entropy for binary two-deletion and two-insertion channels
papers.abstract: Under uniform transmission, we determine the received binary words that maximize input entropy for two-deletion and two-insertion channels. For two deletions the maximizers are exactly the two alternating words at every positive received length. For two insertions the same conclusion holds from received length five onward; we give all smaller cases and exact maximal values. The proof combines an embedding-count identity organized by runs with strict convexity estimates, and a grouping of two-position deletion masks. For every insertion radius we give the complete positive embedding histogram of an alternating received word. We also determine its three-deletion histogram for every length, and certify all three-deletion maximizers through received length twelve and all three-insertion maximizers through length eighteen by exact integer comparison. These computations give precise three-error conjectures with their small-length exceptions.

papers.title: Label Smoothing in Disguise? Gated Knowledge Distillation for Low-Resource Bangla Generation
papers.abstract: Gated knowledge distillation (KD) weights teacher signals per token or example, aiming to trust an imperfect teacher only where it seems reliable. We test two gates: EWAD (entropy-weighted agreement-aware distillation), which gates tokens by teacher confidence, and CHAD (counterfactual harm-aware distillation), which gates examples by gradient alignment with validation data. Across six Bangla-centric tasks, three student models (60M to about 2B parameters), and two teacher families, no gate significantly improves plain KD in 45 comparisons. KD also fails to beat cross-entropy (CE) fine-tuning on gold outputs in 40 single-seed comparisons or three-seed runs on four tasks; CE leads on every summarisation metric. The main benefit of KD is regularisation: over ten fixed epochs, CE students lose 0.030 to 0.044 token-F1 from their early-stopped checkpoint, versus 0.005 to 0.025 for distilled students. Teacher-free label smoothing closes most of this gap. In one comparison, a teacher 0.29 token-F1 worse yields students at most 0.009 worse. Thus, gating may change regularisation strength but has little teacher knowledge to select. Findings are limited to Bangla-centric tasks and small students. We will release code, data splits, predictions, and scores.

papers.title: Uniform cubic bounds for irrational values of the dilogarithm
papers.abstract: We study explicit denominator conditions ensuring the irrationality of the dilogarithm at positive and negative rational points. We prove that $\operatorname{Li}_2(p/q)$ is irrational whenever $q>(4e^4/27)p^3$, and obtain an explicit, slightly smaller threshold for $\operatorname{Li}_2(-p/q)$. The positive argument specializes the Rhin--Viola integral family and uses a uniform estimate for a restricted prime divisor. The negative argument combines the same arithmetic construction with three adjacent integral moments and an explicit maximization. We also give finite-numerator refinements by interpolating certified partition bounds and by introducing a comparison measure with a quadratic tail. In particular, $\operatorname{Li}_2(5/q)$ is irrational for every integer $q\ge418$. The proof separates the established integral and determinant constructions from the parameter estimates and finite certificates used here.

papers.title: Ripple: Deadline-Aware CPU-GPU Sharing for Embodied Inference
papers.abstract: Unified-memory edge devices increasingly run LLM/VLM inference alongside time-critical CPU tasks for perception and control. GPU memory traffic can overwhelm these tasks, yet platforms such as DGX Spark expose neither bandwidth counters nor direct bandwidth regulation. We present Ripple, a CPU-GPU co-scheduler that combines model-derived GPU memory volumes with CPU completion feedback to regulate interference. Ripple divides inference into pausable, layer-based units and translates each CPU job's deadline slack into a GPU-byte budget, admitting work within the budgets of all overlapping jobs. Online updates track changing interference, while deadline-aware pacing and judicious SM footprint narrowing preserve inference progress. Implemented with SGLang engine hooks and a central scheduler, we evaluate Ripple on DGX Spark with four robotic CPU task mixes and LLM/VLM inference. It is the only evaluated approach that consistently meets the 2% CPU deadline-miss target and VLM deadlines across the tested deadline settings while retaining best-effort LLM throughput.

papers.title: Claw-free perfect graphs are chromatic-choosable
papers.abstract: We prove that every claw-free perfect graph $G$ satisfies $\ch(G)=χ(G)=ω(G)$. More strongly, if $S$ is a clique of simplicial vertices of $G$ and $k\geω(G)$, every proper precoloring of $S$ extends to a proper coloring of $G$ from arbitrary lists of size $k$ on $V(G)\setminus S$. The proof has three coloring steps: a mixed-list theorem for cobipartite graphs, a precoloring-extension theorem for elementary graphs built on Galvin's kernel method and a homogeneous-pair exchange argument, and a polynomial method (Combinatorial Nullstellensatz) argument for graphs of interval type in which a Vandermonde factor is transferred across each incomplete pair. The three coloring steps are assembled along the structure theorems of Chvátal--Sbihi, Maffray--Reed and Chudnovsky--Seymour, using double clique cutsets for composition. As a consequence, every perfect line graph is chromatic-choosable, recovering the theorem of Peterson and Woodall. Our precoloring extension theorem also resolves a conjecture posed by Chudnovsky and Seymour.

papers.title: On Sparse Graph Limits for Neural Combinatorial Optimization
papers.abstract: Graph neural networks are often trained on small graphs and deployed on larger ones, raising the question of which graph information must be preserved for combinatorial optimization values to transfer across sizes. We establish size-transfer guarantees for normalized graph optimization values using finite collections of energy features. For affine objectives, including MAX-CUT, coloring defect, and independent-set density, differences in task value are controlled by discrepancies in normalized scalar energy probes on all bounded-degree graphs. For general Lipschitz objectives, such as those with balance penalties, an additional representation error appears; this error vanishes on hyperfinite graph families but can remain bounded away from zero on expanders. Thus, at fixed degree bound, state space, Lipschitz constant, and target accuracy, a finite energy representation independent of graph size suffices universally for affine tasks and asymptotically for general Lipschitz tasks on hyperfinite families. These results yield prediction guarantees under explicit conditions on encoder accuracy, readout stability, and representation coverage, together with statistical generalization bounds. Theoretically, we prove Shapley-Folkman bounds with sharp parameter dependence, including a dimension-free $\ell_2$ regime, and realize the resulting energy features with a fixed-weight message-passing network using random node initialization on bounded-treewidth graphs. Experiments with exact solvers and trained models test the resulting transfer guarantees.

papers.title: Synergetic Autonomous Intelligence: Three Axioms for Recursive Semi-Closed Learning
papers.abstract: We introduce Synergetic Autonomous Intelligence (SAI), a theory and design program for learning systems that form, preserve, revise, and compose relations while continuing to learn. SAI is built on three axioms: consequential distinctions must not become orphaned (U); identity is determined by future-faithful continuation under a declared contract (I); and unresolved defects are repaired by the least lawful local completion at the lowest admitted grade (L). We model a model, agent, tool, team, or environment boundary as a recursive semi-closed system with a Kernel-Ring representation, a Compile-Open-Participate cycle, and a typed residual comparing actual with claimed continuation. Under explicit finite or affine contracts, we establish relative consistency and conditional non-redundancy of U/I/L, characterize a contract-relative semantic quotient, construct an exact joint stochastic refinement, derive a constrained residual contraction, prove finite-horizon continued-service viability, and give an executed-intervention identification result with an observational-confounding boundary. We define GRC-Close as the generative and repair schema for this contract. The framework also gives finite contracts for action-effect-feedback loop re-entry, partial failure, duplicate-effect idempotency, replay, concurrent delivery, causal uncertainty, and threshold-radix state representation. KREIT, the Kernel-Ring Equilibrium Information Theory layer, treats information as a typed, resource-bounded distinction; the control layer authorizes, executes, audits, and updates actions across cloud-edge-end scales. These results establish a common contract-level vocabulary for representation, relation, memory, action, communication, explanation, coordination, and growth, while marking the assumptions and open boundaries required for later generalization.

papers.title: Hi-CoLA: High Confidence Lower Bound Approximation Based Reinforcement Learning for Flex-Route Transit Operation Control
papers.abstract: This paper studies safe policy improvement for real-time operation control of flex-route transit (FRT) systems, where robustness is critical and any performance decrease is undesirable. While reinforcement learning (RL) has shown strong empirical success, its adoption remains limited in safety and cost critical applications, such as intelligent transportation, since learned policies lack statistically certified performance guarantees before deployment. In this paper, we propose the High Confidence Lower Bound Approximation (Hi-CoLA) RL framework, which combines importance sampling and concentration inequalities with a differentiable surrogate network to efficiently estimate the high-confidence performance lower bound and optimize it via policy gradient for robust performance improvement. On the FRT operation control problem, Hi-CoLA outperforms state-of-the-art offline and safe RL methods in both average and tail-risk performance. A case study on an actual route in Chicago, implemented in the SUMO simulator, serves as a proof of concept. Hi-CoLA enhances real-time FRT control with guaranteed performance and is broadly applicable to other safety critical decision-making scenarios.

papers.title: Where Beam Search Loses Top-Ranked Items:First-Step Coverage in Generative Recommendation
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation can reproduce a wider beam's ranked output with roughly half the prefix-capacity budget by reallocating retention capacity across semantic-ID positions. We identify a \emph{first-step coverage bottleneck}: across six full-test settings of the TIGER generative recommender spanning three domains and two identifier constructions, every pruned exact top-10 path is first lost at the initial decoding step. An exact-catalog reference isolates search losses and guides a controlled budget intervention. Moving width to the first step raises Search Recall@10 by 0.96--10.90 percentage points at Beam-50's unchanged budget. Across all 77,373 test users with residual-quantized variational autoencoder (RQ-VAE) tokenization, the reallocated schedule reproduces Beam-100's ordered top-10 at nominal budgets of 151 rather than 301, without retraining or changing identifiers or scores. Matched-output timing saves 6.35--6.39\% of decoder latency; profiling identifies the execution costs that limit the translation from reduced search work to runtime savings. Larger-candidate experiments reveal how output size changes retention requirements. These findings make budget placement an actionable serving decision: locate ranking loss, redirect search capacity, and preserve downstream inputs before increasing uniform beam width.

papers.title: Rogue waves in the dam-break problem for the Kundu--Eckhaus equation
papers.abstract: We study rogue wave formation in the dam-break problem for the Kundu--Eckhaus equation with deterministic and randomly perturbed box initial data. For the unperturbed real box, the gauge transformation and Galilean invariance relate the intensity evolution to that of the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation. The Kundu--Eckhaus parameter determines the phase, the real shift of the discrete spectrum and the drift velocity. We compare uniform, Gaussian and Laplace perturbations with equal variance and the same correlation scale in the underlying Gaussian field. At the larger perturbation strengths considered, the Laplace perturbations yield larger mean maximum intensities and higher exceedance probabilities for the normalized intensity at the final simulation time, but smaller amplification relative to the initial maximum intensity.

papers.title: Grounding Across Views: Cross-View Referring Reasoning for Visual Grounding
papers.abstract: Cross-view object geo-localization (CVOGL) aims to localize a target in a satellite image from an observation captured under another viewpoint. Existing methods typically specify the query with a click point or bounding box, marking the target region but underusing the semantic attributes and relations conveyed by natural language. Moreover, referring expressions are often viewpoint-dependent, making query-view descriptions difficult to ground directly in the satellite image. In this paper, we formulate cross-view visual grounding (CVVG), extending conventional point- or box-prompted CVOGL to instance grounding jointly guided by a referring expression and a visual exemplar. We present GAV (Grounding Across Views), a view-aware framework for selectively transferring visual and linguistic evidence across views. Its core is view-aware referring reasoning: target-centered descriptions are derived from the marked query image, checked for target-category consistency, and augmented with a direction-free role cue. Exemplar prompting, cross-view alignment, and scene-level discrimination ground this semantic evidence in a satellite instance. GAV achieves a new state of the art on MoP-UAV with 62.55% Acc@0.5. We also introduce CVOGL-Text, a benchmark for text-guided grounding from street- and drone-view queries to satellite images. GAV outperforms the click-point baseline by 7.09 and 6.79 Acc@0.25 points on the street- and drone-view splits, respectively, demonstrating robustness to larger viewpoint gaps. The code and annotations will be publicly released.

papers.title: Massively parallel Schwarz methods for the high-frequency Helmholtz equation with O(k) convergence
papers.abstract: We develop a one-level restricted additive Schwarz solver with perfectly matched layer transmission conditions (RAS--PML) for high-frequency Helmholtz systems. For problems with ${O}(k^d)$ unknowns, $d=2,3$, the solver uses Cartesian decompositions and ${O}(k^d)$ concurrent local solves for a single right-hand side, where $k$ is the wavenumber. Starting from the convergence theory for fixed decompositions established in~\texttt{arXiv:2404.02156}, we address the growing cost {as $k$ increases} of local solves through a nested RAS--PML construction. Under suitable stability and contraction assumptions, we prove that sufficiently accurate recursive local solves preserve convergence of the outer iteration. We also prove that a single inner iteration at each non-terminal level yields a correction algebraically equivalent to one-level RAS--PML, provided that the hierarchy-induced finest local problems and composite restriction and weighted extension operators are retained. This equivalence provides a hierarchical interpretation and permits a direct implementation without recursive transfers. We assess the one-level solver using PML and overlap widths of order ${O}(k^{-1}\log k)$. Constant-coefficient experiments cover $300\leq k\leq19200$ in two dimensions and $60\leq k\leq780$ in three dimensions, reaching $1.47\times10^9$ and $4.75\times10^8$ complex unknowns, respectively. Richardson iteration counts grow approximately linearly with $k$ over these ranges, while total parallel runtime, including setup and solution, exhibits near-linear growth at the larger tested wavenumbers. Further experiments assess the effects of mesh refinement and heterogeneous media.

papers.title: Change the Funnel, Not Who May Submit: Engineering Peer Review for the Flood
papers.abstract: Every reviewer knows the feeling: more papers each cycle, three full reviews for each of them, and a suspicion that near the accept line the outcome is luck. The numbers bear it out. NeurIPS received 30,709 submissions in 2026, more than three times as many as in 2021, and reviewing them took some 184,000 expert hours, or 92 years of researchers' time. Three-quarters of those hours went to papers that were rejected. And when NeurIPS twice had the same papers reviewed by two committees, the second rejected half of what the first accepted. Conferences are responding by limiting who may submit. We simulated that answer, and an alternative, in a model calibrated to the NeurIPS experiments. The limits save little and select no better, and those based on a past acceptance fall mostly on new authors. The alternative changes how papers are judged, spending full reads only where a decision turns on them. In a staged funnel, an automated quality check first turns back papers that are not ready. The rest are ranked by their value, from short summaries, by readers that each submission brings. Only the finalists get a full read, which checks their claims and settles the final ranking. The staged funnel needs a little over half of today's expert hours, accepts 95.5% of papers in the top 3-10% (against 74% today), and makes nearly every top-0.5% paper a spotlight or oral. And because every paper brings its own reader, the funnel keeps pace with the flood.

papers.title: Multi-Turn Semantic Caching for Low-Cost LLM Serving
papers.abstract: Semantic caching lowers the cost of serving large language models (LLMs) by reusing stored responses for similar requests. In multi-turn conversations, whether a cached response is acceptable depends on both conversations' histories, which embedding similarity of requests and histories predicts poorly (AUC 0.62--0.74 on five workloads). We therefore learn the \emph{reuse risk}, the probability that a cached response is unacceptable, from judge feedback, and choose a budgeted set of conversation states to cache by weighing the generation cost a reuse avoids against a price for unacceptable reuse. We propose CUCB-SC-MT, which learns a cache from logged conversations with a suboptimality guarantee, and CLCB-LS-MT, which learns online and has $\tilde O(\sqrt N)$ regret over $N$ requests when conversation states recur. On math-tutoring (SocraTeach) and movie-ticketing (Taskmaster-3) conversations, both achieve lower loss than prior semantic caching approaches: ContextCache, multi-turn variants of ElastiCache and vCache, and single-turn semantic caching at every cache budget. With 1,000 cache entries, CLCB-LS-MT avoids 35--41\% of the generation cost through acceptable reuses, against at most 22--25\% for the baselines, and lowers estimated serving latency by 19--35\%.

papers.title: CuPH: Parallel Cubical Persistent Homology via Level-Synchronous Component Tracking
papers.abstract: Persistent homology (PH) is a mathematically principled multi-scale topological descriptor of shape and connectivity in data. It is widely applied in image classification, segmentation, and shape analysis across medical and aerial imaging, providing structural information that pixel-wise deep learning may overlook. Standard cubical PH decomposes an image into cubical cells (vertices, edges, and squares) and reduces them sequentially in filtration order. This sequential reduction has $Θ(n)$ parallel depth for an $n$-pixel image, limiting within-image GPU parallelism and constraining its use in topology-aware deep learning. We introduce CuPH, a GPU-based parallel algorithm for computing cubical PH on 2D images that operates directly on pixels rather than cubical cells. CuPH buckets pixels by filtration values, activates them with a level-synchronous sweep, and tracks connected components with a lock-free union-find method. We prove that CuPH produces persistence diagrams identical to standard cubical PH on integer inputs, with a stability bound for floating-point inputs. CuPH reduces parallel depth from $Θ(n)$ to $O(L\log n)$ for an image with $L$ intensity levels. We implement the level sweep as a single CUDA kernel, eliminating cross-level kernel-launch overhead. Empirically, CuPH is $18.6$--$99.6\times$ faster than the existing GPU baseline (CMP). As a drop-in PH backend, CuPH accelerates topology-aware classification ($4.2$--$16.7\times$) and segmentation ($8.3$--$44\times$) while preserving accuracy. It also enables computing full-image PH losses on high-resolution images, improving segmentation Dice by $2.2$--$4.6$ points over patch-local PH baselines and accelerating training by $25$--$31\times$.

papers.title: Optimally Weighted Constrained Shadow Tomography for Reduced Density Matrices
papers.abstract: Accurate measurement of reduced density matrices (RDMs) is central to quantum simulations of many-fermion systems, but the required measurement resources remain a significant challenge. Constrained shadow tomography (CST) combines randomized measurements with $N$-representability conditions to reconstruct physically valid RDMs from limited measurement data. Here we improve CST by orthogonalizing the measurement constraints and using the resulting singular values to determine the relative weight of each independent measurement direction according to how strongly it is sampled by the quantum computer. These optimally weighted constraints are incorporated into the semidefinite program through a least-squares objective implemented with a Schur-complement relaxation. We demonstrate the approach for hydrogen chains on a quantum simulator and for azobenzene on a quantum processor. In both cases, optimally weighted CST systematically improves the accuracy of the reconstructed 2-RDM without increasing the measurement budget, providing a more measurement-efficient approach to partial tomography for quantum simulations of correlated fermions.

papers.title: Chiral Unidirectional Resonances Enabled by Complete Coherent Radiation Control
papers.abstract: Optical resonances are commonly characterized by their quality factors, while their radiation exhibits richer properties associated with polarization and directional selectivity. Chiral and unidirectional guided resonances exploit complementary aspects of radiation, motivating a unified framework for controlling polarization and directionality together. Here we develop such a framework and introduce chiral unidirectional resonances (CURs) with arbitrarily high radiative quality factors and near-unity single-channel selectivity. We further extend this theory to guide the geometric design of arbitrary coherent emission states with prescribed radiative lifetimes. In addition, we establish scaling laws for the lifetime and radiation-state fidelity, and demonstrate robust chiral unidirectional emission over a finite momentum region. Our demonstrations provide a basis for single-sided circularly polarized light sources and polarization-matched optical coupling.

papers.title: Robust Safety Assurance for Robotic Swarms Using Decentralized Collision Verification
papers.abstract: In this paper we present the methodologies, results, and analysis used to deploy a decentralized safety verification algorithm on a robotic swarm to prevent collisions at runtime in an outdoor environment. Typically, approaches toward verification of swarms of cyber-physical systems (CPS) are evaluated solely in numerical simulations or in highly controlled, noiseless indoor environments. Our efforts to implement collision avoidance on a real swarm system outdoors have revealed that the underlying algorithmic assumptions juxtaposed against the implementation details of the target system are critical factors in a method's efficacy in the real world. Here we modify, enhance, and analyze a decentralized reachability-based method for collision avoidance on a size, weight, and power-constrained uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) swarm with the objective of illustrating the challenges of real-world CPS deployments as well as provide guidance for researchers in this space. Verification performance, resource utilization, and timing data were gathered over the course of 140 total outdoor vehicle flights, including 6 swarm flights composed of 8 UAVs, and used to improve collision-avoidance performance as experimentation progressed. Our extensive experiments show that the proposed decentralized runtime verification approach can efficiently verify the safety of multiple UAVs in real-time and help all agents take safe actions to avoid collisions. On average, each agent, using our open-source safety_checker library, takes approximately 500-520 ms to verify its safety for the next 4 s into the future, in which the reachable set broadcast time dominates the total verification time (~300-500 ms).

papers.title: VeilFL: Two-Stage Accountability for Anonymous Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Anonymous credentials can hide which registered client participates in federated learning, but their unlinkability also makes repeated misconduct difficult to associate. We present VeilFL, a two-aggregator protocol that adds staged accountability to PINE (USENIX Security '24). Each submission binds two private PINE messages, a round-specific pseudonym, and a tracing pair to the same hidden credential secret. This design enables detection of duplicate submissions within a round without introducing a persistent identifier for normal participation. VeilFL implements accountability in two stages. After a confirmed duplicate or joint PINE rejection, a threshold tracing committee reveals a stable handle that links faults associated with the same credential. The client's registered identity is recoverable only after the public log records the requisite number of linked faults and a separate threshold committee authorizes identification. Accepted and unopened submissions remain unlinkable under the stated assumptions. This work establishes submission binding and duplicate detection, anonymity, fault non-frameability, controlled two-stage opening, and preservation of PINE's privacy and validity guarantees. In the prototype implementation, creating a submission requires a median of 2.11 ms, while verification requires 3.01 ms. Batch verification reduces the cost to 1.86 ms per submission for a batch of 1,000. The public part of each submission is 608 bytes, with 1,248 bytes of additional VeilFL protocol data across the two aggregator submissions. Each opening stage completes within 4.3 ms for the different committee configurations.

papers.title: A relative version of Weinstein's morphism
papers.abstract: We introduce a relative version of Weinstein's morphism associated to a Lagrangian submanifold \(L\) of a closed symplectic manifold \((M,ω)\). We construct a homomorphism \[ \mathcal{A}^{(L,α)}\colon π_{1}\bigl(\operatorname{Ham}_0(M,L)\bigr) \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}/\mathcal{P}_{2}(M,ω), \] and establish its basic properties. We compute the invariant in several examples, including latitude circles in \(S^2\), and more generally, Lagrangian fibers in toric manifolds. These computations provide obstructions to Ha\-mil\-to\-nian isotopy of Lagrangian submanifolds and detect nontrivial, and in some cases infinite-order, elements in the homotopy groups of their Hamiltonian stabilizers.

papers.title: QVR3D: Query-Guided Visual Reasoning for Training-Free 3D Grounding
papers.abstract: 3D visual grounding localizes objects in 3D scenes from natural language descriptions, requiring reasoning over semantics, spatial relationships, and multi-view observations. Training-free approaches avoid costly annotations but often rely on explicit scene transformation or scene-level frame selection, which may waste limited visual capacity on query-irrelevant regions. We observe that effective grounding should prioritize observations that provide evidence for the query rather than uniformly represent the entire scene. Based on this insight, we introduce QVR3D, a query-guided visual reasoning framework that operates on RGB-D observations using off-the-shelf foundation models. QVR3D combines Query-Guided Maximum Coverage (QGMC) for selecting complementary query-relevant views with Grounding Probability Estimation (GPE) that integrates instance confidence, attribute consistency, and relationship consistency. The framework supports both single- and multi-object grounding without task-specific adaptation. Experiments on ScanRefer and Nr3D achieve state-of-the-art zero-shot performance, while QGMC also improves frame efficiency across multiple 3D vision-language tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/jwliao1209/QVR3D.

papers.title: On the Time-Domain Waveforms Leading to Frequency Comb Spectra
papers.abstract: Frequency-comb spectra can arise from distinct time-domain waveforms. We develop a Fourier-based framework that relates waveform symmetry, regularity, and modulation to the structure of overtone- and sideband frequency combs. Analytical derivations show that symmetry determines the allowed harmonic orders, while waveform regularity governs spectral decay: discontinuities produce $n^{-1}$ scaling, derivative discontinuities yield $n^{-2}$ scaling, and smooth nonlinear mappings can produce rapidly decaying harmonics. For modulated carriers, we distinguish consecutive sidebands, symmetry-induced missing orders, and nonuniformly spaced frequency components. In particular, spectral sparsity does not necessarily imply a nonuniform frequency lattice. Comparisons of analytical coefficients with calculated time-domain signals and Fourier spectra establish the correspondence between waveform properties and spectral signatures. The results provide a mathematical basis for interpreting frequency-comb structures while identifying the limitations of magnitude-only spectra in determining their underlying physical mechanisms.

papers.title: Growth of global science: reflections on measurability and scientometric insights
papers.abstract: Global science has become much larger and more interconnected in recent years. Such a complex and adaptive social system defies any attempt to systematically and comprehensively measure or monitor its growth and evolution. Yet, as it continues to expand and enhance its public value, effective evidence-based assessment has become increasingly critical for understanding its dynamics and managing the system. This paper offers a framework for addressing system-level measurability challenges. Inspired by Derek de Solla Prices pioneering scientometric work in the 1960s, this paper addresses analytical issues related to current measurements of the systems expansion since the turn of the 21st century. Our empirical analysis of global science dynamics presents new macro-level data on several observable megatrends in research publication output worldwide. Acknowledging the limited analytical scope of these trend data to understand the dynamics of global science, we outline currently available options to improve system-level measurability under conditions of ambiguity and uncertainty. Looking forward, we discuss likely future directions to establish integrated, multi-stakeholder measurement infrastructures.

papers.title: Is That Clear? The Impacts of Clarifying Questions on Human-LLM Interaction
papers.abstract: LLM assistants increasingly ask clarifying questions (CQs) to elicit preferences and tailor recommendations. Although prior work emphasizes improvements in answer quality and user experience, how CQs shape users' subsequent engagement and reliance remains unclear. We conducted a controlled experiment (N=180) across six everyday decision scenarios, comparing human-LLM interaction with and without CQs. We further manipulated whether responses violated explicit constraints and whether violations occurred in the sub-decisions the CQs addressed, while preserving elicited preferences. CQs increased perceived understanding and satisfaction, yet participants spent less time reviewing and evaluating responses and accepted more responses unchanged, including erroneous ones. Within the CQ condition, participants more often accepted responses containing CQ-adjacent violations than nonadjacent violations. These findings demonstrate that LLM's proactive CQs shape subsequent engagement and reliance with preference elicitation. We discuss implications for designing and evaluating proactive assistants that support continued user scrutiny of answers alongside personalization.

papers.title: The Eleven Questions : March 2016 - October 2026
papers.abstract: We review the eleven open questions in Appendix H of Farina's manuscript on entire solutions of the Allen-Cahn equation (dated March 9, 2016).

papers.title: Scute: Exact Batched Serving for PEFT Adapters Beyond LoRA
papers.abstract: Existing serving systems for large language models batch requests for many different LoRA adapters on one GPU. However, these systems reject adapters from other parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods such as DoRA, (IA), VeRA and OFT. One solution to this is to convert these adapters to LoRA, but this induces a significant memory and accuracy cost. Instead, we show that, under some modifications, a batched LoRA kernel can serve all of these methods exactly and efficiently. We achieve this by writing each method in one normal form, a LoRA computation with six slots for an adapter's own vectors and matrices. Some slots can merge into an adapter's weights at load time; the others remain live and induce a cost. We give ways to efficiently pay this cost and predict it from a zero-parameter byte model. We package this system, Scute, and build it on top of vLLM. Scute serves all five methods, coming as checkpoints from the Hugging Face PEFT library, in one batch, and it matches that library with a mean error of at most 1.5% of each adapter's effect. Under a burst of requests on an RTX A6000, a mix of these methods takes 5-17% more decode time than the same number of LoRA adapters. Furthermore, using Scute, the same GPU can serve 64 to 1024 (IA) and VeRA adapters at 1.5x to at least 2.5x the request rate of their LoRA conversions.

papers.title: Numerical Embeddings for CTR Prediction: A Taxonomy, Unified Benchmark, and Open-Source FuxiCTR Extension
papers.abstract: Numerical embeddings map scalar features into vectors before a click-through rate (CTR) backbone combines the fields. To our knowledge, NumEmbBench is the first open benchmark dedicated to comparing numerical embeddings for CTR prediction. We classify 18 configurations into six mechanism-based families and evaluate them through one FuxiCTR interface. After equal-budget validation tuning, we compare frozen configurations on three datasets, nine backbones, and five seeds under a shared train-only z-score protocol. DEER has the best mean rank, but six methods lead at least one dataset--backbone setting. A matched native-scale test changes the winner in 11 of 27 settings, while paired latency measurements show that accuracy and inference cost need not move together. Code and per-seed results: https://github.com/YH-learning/NumEmbBench

papers.title: Understanding Work/Life Balance Through Mathematical Model
papers.abstract: Work/life balance (WLB) remains a central yet elusive concept in social and organizational sciences, often described qualitatively without a unified quantitative framework. To address this gap, a novel compartmental mathematical model is proposed that formalizes WLB as a dynamic population-level phenomenon. The individuals are categorized into 4 compartments, namely, regularly employed, temporarily employed, imbalanced (infected), and balanced (recovered), representing balanced and imbalanced states. Role-based complaints govern the transitions between states, the conflict conversion rates of these complaints, and the recovery rate.
